extracted.intended_audience: aspiring novelists, literary critics, and students of fiction technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on novel method: choosing and managing point of view, when to use scenic (pictorial) vs dramatic/panoramic presentation, placing and preparing scenes, and controlling authorial tone and irony to shape reader identification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author voice vs character voice (point of view usage)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes the author speaks in his own voice, sometimes through one of the people in the book—e.g., much of Madame Bovary is told through Emma's viewpoint; at other times the author 'faces the reader in person' describing landscape, manners, or behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about which voice is operating at any moment; use the author's voice to reproduce what is in his mind and use a character's voice to convey the colour of things as they appear to that character. Avoid careless or unexplained shifts that deflect reader attention. Examples: author describes countryside in his own language; then retreats and uses Emma's mind to color the landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic (pictorial) vs dramatic treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene may be treated pictorially—focused on a single hour and bathed in a character's mood—or dramatically—presenting visible and audible facts that could be staged without loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose pictorial treatment when you want the reader to feel the character's inner atmosphere (e.g., Emma's experience at the ball). Choose dramatic treatment when the objective facts themselves (dialogue, crowd, speeches) are to convey the impression (e.g., the comices/cattle-show). Mixing is possible but must be managed so each effect is preserved; note that staging a pictorially-rendered scene may destroy its book-unique effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scenic vs panoramic presentation (scene vs summary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between close, particular scenes and broad, panoramic surveys. Some novels lean toward a concatenation of scenes; others toward broad surveys of society (Thackeray's panoramas).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch how alternation is managed: scenes usually yield to chronicle or summary which then prepares the next occasion. Use panorama when you need a sweeping, survey view; use scenic when you need concentrated immediacy. Expect and plan transitions between the two so the reader is not jarred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene necessity and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene must be wanted and do something specific; a scene that 'for lack of preparation fails to make its effect' is a weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place a scene at the point where everything is ready for it to illuminate a new face of the subject and advance the action. Avoid gratuitous or unprepared scenes; each scene should start an interest, raise a question, or serve as a climax/resolution in the scheme of the book. Example anti-pattern: a scene that merely occupies space without forwarding meaning or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center of vision / POV choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide with which mind (if any) the writer will identify—whose inner life will be revealed—and avoid haphazard plunges into other minds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject can be rendered through a single figure, keep to that centre; unnecessary or casual shifts into other characters' minds confuse and change focus without compensating gain. However, occasional justified shifts are allowable when they serve structure (e.g., providing material needed later).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the novel's subject (portrait vs drama)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the true subject is a portrait of a character (a study of a nature) or a drama (an interaction/conflict between character and environment), since this determines method and setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose setting, incidents, and emphasis according to the chosen subject. If the novel is a portrait, elements are chosen to illuminate the character; if the novel is a drama, emphasize the collision of wills and the question of outcome. Example: Madame Bovary is not merely a portrait of Emma but a picture/drama of a woman in a narrow provincial world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering setting as integral (setting equals character prominence)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the subject requires it, the environment must be as distinct and thoroughly characterized as the protagonist—setting can be integral, not mere background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat scenery and local types with as much intensity as the heroine; if the provincial scene is essential to the subject, render its individuality sharply (e.g., Yonville in Madame Bovary). The setting should help make the portrait or drama intelligible and visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing transitions between subjective and authorial/objective viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts from a character's inner view to the author's detached account must be handled without awkwardness; naked contrasts between subjective experience and external commentary are disconcerting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disguise transitions so they are smooth and do not break the reader's shared immersion. Avoid overtly 'going behind' a character and then openly presuming an outside critical stance. Anti-pattern: abrupt or boastful authorial intrusions that damage the story's illusion (Thackeray's occasional open maltreatment is cited as a deliberate but risky exception).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of irony and authorial distance to control reader identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a measured aloofness—a 'hint of irony'—so the reader can enter a character's consciousness yet still perceive the author's valuation and broader view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the character's subjectivity intelligible but subtly qualified by the author's ironic tone; irony allows the author to supersede a limited vision when necessary without dislocating the reader. Don’t state moral judgments plainly; let tone and implication supply them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author supplies perception when protagonist is inadequate
rubrics_metrics.description: When the protagonist's intelligence or wit is too feeble to reveal the world fully, the author's mind must supply what is lacking to create a complete picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare such interventions carefully so they do not feel like arbitrary substitutions of values. Keep the transition unobtrusive and maintain a consistent standard so the reader accepts the supplementary viewpoint as part of the story's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing and foreshadowing via other characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use episodes from other characters' lives (e.g., Charles's history) to frame the narrative and to prepare impressions or resources needed for later climactic payoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include background episodes only when they are required for later effects (e.g., to make the husband's later discovery plausible and emotionally effective). What appears irrelevant early may be necessary to hold the end in readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and consistency of method
rubrics_metrics.description: The writer must be 'consistent on some plan' and 'allow himself no more latitude than he requires'—method should be chosen to suit the subject and used scrupulously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the few essential methods that serve the novel's theme and avoid gratuitous variety. Consistency of plan gives unity and preserves effect; variety is permissible but should be restricted to what the story demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layering and fusion of methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods are few and simple but can be alternated, united, imposed one on another—creating layers and stratifications in the treatment of a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore combinations (e.g., blending dramatic action with pictorial description, or one point of view blended with another) to enrich texture, but monitor how these layers interact so the reader can follow the design. Analyze how method tends to be laid upon method to reveal the novelist's imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene as primary device to start interest and complete action
rubrics_metrics.description: The scene 'holds the place of honour'—it's the readiest means of starting interest, raising questions, and recurring for climaxes; scenes often articulate the structure of the book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open with a scene to hook curiosity and distribute scenes so each contributes to the book's articulation (examples: the ball, the comices, the cathedral interview, the deathbed). Use rapid summary between scenes to carry the book toward the next climax. Ensure each scene 'completes what it began' and yields increasing effect on rereading.
